newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria uses $133 mln of Bradys in privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria uses $133 mln of Bradys in privatisation.

text.p: Bulgarian Brady bonds with a total par value of $133 million were used as a means of payment in privatisation deals by November 30, 1996, the finance ministry said.

"The Bulgarian government received Brady bonds worth $133 million as payment in debt-to-equity swaps by November 30, 1996," head of the treasury and debt department at the finance ministry Plamen Oresharski told Reuters.
"These bonds were reported to the debt agent for redemption," he added.
In 1995 some $117 million of Brady bonds used in privatisation were Front Loaded Interest Reduction Bonds (FLIRBs) and $2 million were Collateralised Discount Bonds (DISCs).
In 1996 all $14 million of Brady bonds used were DISCs.

Bulgaria issued on July 28, 1994 three types of Brady bonds - FLIRBs, DISCs and Interest Arrears Bonds (IABs), with a total par value of $5.1 billion in exchange for its $8.16 billion debt to commercial creditors.

DISCs and FLIRBs are eligible for debt-to-equity swaps in Bulgaria with DISCs at their par value and FLIRBs at 50 percent of their par value. Payment is usually due within a month of the deal being signed.
According to debt-to-equity swaps regulations up to 50 percent of a privatisation deal can be paid with Brady bonds.

Brady bonds have been used in few deals last year, which include the sell-offs of construction company Glavbulgarstroi to GBS-Privat and sanitary and industrial fittings maker Vidima to American Standard Co Inc.
Bulgaria privatised 509 enterprises worth 95.93 billion levs in 1996, the Privatisation Agency said in its annual report, after 309 deals in 1995.

Privatisation proceeds are a key source of revenue for the state budget. A tough monetary regime proposed by the International Monetary Fund to stabilise Bulgaria's crumbling financial system is due to be introduced in June.

Bulgaria's foreign debt payments due this year amount to $992.2 million and the country hopes to receive at least $1 billion from sell-offs of some 1,000 firms this year under a draft privatisation programme aimed to compensate delays over the past seven year.
